Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
This looks like early 2019 or the end of March 2019, with a policy rate of 2.40%, unemployment at 4.0%, and a 10-year yield of 2.69%.

The fed funds rate of 2.40% matches the period from December 2018 to mid-2019. The 10-year yield of 2.69% fits March 2019, when it was about 2.41%, or alternatively January 2019, when it was about 2.63%. The 2-year yield of 2.50% fits January or February 2019.

Headline CPI at 1.52% YoY matches January 2019, when it was 1.6%. The unemployment rate of 4.0% matches January 2019. Payrolls averaged about 240k over three months, which fits January 2019 given the revised December figure of about 222k and a January figure of about 304k.

US equities returned +5.8% in the month, with a -2.8% 6-month return. That fits January 2019, when the S&P gained about 8%, though February 2019 gained about 3%. The 6-month return of -2.8% fits January 2019, since the period began in July 2018 and included the December selloff. The 12-month return of +3.5% also fits. Gold's 3-month return of +7.2% fits too.

The VIX at 14.7 fits February 2019 (about 14.8), though the January figure was about 16.6. A 1-month equity return of +5.8% with a 3-month return of +4.8% suggests the month after the December low. Counting back, November through January would give roughly +4.8%, with January at +8%, so February may fit better. A 3-month window of December through February would be about -9% + 8% + 3%, which is negative, so that does not match. A window of November through January would be +1.8% - 9% + 8%, which is also not +4.8%. A window of January through March would be 8% + 3% + 1.9%, roughly 13%, which is too high. February's 1-month return of 3% does not match +5.8% either.

Alternatively, the snapshot could be February 2019 with some difference in how returns are computed, but the dollar and the 12-month figures fit that period as well. I'll go with February 2019.
